title: Find the user behind a design
kit: A familiar tool, tape measure, pencil and student packet.
entry: Start here with a familiar tool. Work in pairs and switch interviewer after the first observation.
measure: Observe one use of the tool. Record who used it, what it acted on, and one dimension or count you can check.
plan: Sketch the tool as used. Label its input and the job the user wants done.
make: Have your partner perform the job. Record a point where the tool helps and a point where the user has to adjust.
test: Give a second user the same job. Compare the two observations and refine your statement of need.
exit: Name the user, the job, and one piece of evidence that would justify a design change.
guide: Accept a need supported by observation. Ask what another user would do differently.

title: Design and test a phone holder
kit: Per pair: one folder, 12 in of tape, scissors, ruler, rigid phone blank, timer.
entry: Identify the workbench user and one limit. Use the same rigid blank for both trials.
measure: Measure the blank’s width and thickness to the nearest 1/16 in. Mark its display side.
plan: Sketch two holders. Label the support, opening, and a critical dimension. Choose the more promising design.
make: Fold and tape the first holder. Set it on the bench with the blank’s face visible. Keep enough material for a revision.
test: Time an unsupported hold up to 30 s. Remove and replace the blank one-handed three times. Change one feature and repeat both tests.
exit: Which change would you keep? Give a dimension with units and compare the two versions’ hold times or successful cycles.
guide: Observe each student measuring. A holder can stand for 30 s and still fail retrieval. Ask for both results.

title: Lay out a pattern another builder can use
kit: Holder from Task 1.2, graph paper, folder stock, ruler, scissors.
entry: Provide a holder or an unfolded sample if the class enters here.
measure: Measure a flat pattern and the usable sheet. Mark cut and fold lines differently.
plan: Draw front and side views. Include width, height, and the opening. Mark which view supplies each measurement.
make: Fit copies of the pattern on one sheet without overlap. Count whole parts and compare with an area-only estimate.
test: Give your views to a partner. Ask them to locate a fold and one hidden dimension. Correct any ambiguity.
exit: Show the number of whole parts per sheet. Explain one reason it can differ from the area estimate.
guide: Look for whole parts, orientation, and waste. Accept different layouts if every part fits.

title: Write an organizer brief for a user
kit: Real items to store, an existing organizer or photo, ruler and student packet.
entry: Provide the contact or role of a user who can test the finished organizer.
measure: Measure three items. Ask the user which is hardest to retrieve. Record a quote or observed action.
plan: List the job, two measurable criteria, and a material or space limit. Sketch the area available.
make: Compare an existing organizer with the brief. Have the user try its arrangement with the actual items.
test: Read the brief back to the user. Replace a vague word such as easy with an action you can observe.
exit: Give one user requirement, its test, and the observation that led you to choose it.
guide: Listen for a user-defined priority and a repeatable test. Have the user resolve conflicting priorities.

title: Choose an organizer layout
kit: Three measured items, user brief, grid paper, ruler, cardboard sample.
entry: Use the prior user brief or supply a brief and the objects to store.
measure: Measure wall thickness and the outer footprint. Calculate the clear width left for storage.
plan: Each partner sketches a different layout. Compare both against the same criteria in the packet decision table.
make: Mark the two layouts full size on paper. Place the items inside and trace the hand’s access route.
test: Test each layout for fit and retrieval. Use the results to choose a design and update its dimensions.
exit: Which design won? Show one clearance calculation and name a trade-off the user accepts.
guide: Check for wall thickness in the arithmetic. A winning score needs a physical fit check.

title: Build the organizer prototype
kit: Selected layout, cardboard, ruler, tape, scissors and actual stored objects.
entry: Supply the approved layout, user criteria, and objects before cutting.
measure: Transfer dimensions from one edge. Label parts and measure the actual thickness of one wall.
plan: Create a cut list. Decide which part to fit first and which joint to leave accessible for inspection.
make: Cut and dry-fit the base and walls. Check the actual objects, then fasten the parts. Record one departure from the plan.
test: Have a partner check a bay against its design dimension. Mark any interference or inaccessible item.
exit: Record a planned and an actual dimension. Explain whether the difference matters to this user.
guide: Inspect the dry fit before fastening. Require an as-built measurement and units.

title: Run a user test and select a revision
kit: Prototype, objects, user criteria, stopwatch and spare stock.
entry: Start with a working prototype or use a supplied organizer and a written brief.
measure: Choose a score for retrieval, such as successful attempts out of three. Record a timed baseline if time matters to the user.
plan: Agree on the starting arrangement and directions. Avoid coaching the tester during the trial.
make: Run the test with the actual user. Record what happened on each attempt and one comment about access.
test: Repeat a trial to check that the problem recurs. Mark the feature you will change in the next version.
exit: Use the trials to defend one revision. Name a second possible cause you checked.
guide: Look for actual trial results and consistent starting conditions. Do not require success on the first build.

title: Hand over the revised organizer
kit: Prototype, test record, spare stock, ruler and user.
entry: Bring a tested organizer and a written user request. If either is absent, use the preceding lesson first.
measure: Calculate material used or cost from a supplied classroom price. Label price assumptions.
plan: Choose one revision from the test and mark its new dimension on the drawing.
make: Modify the organizer. Have the same user repeat the original test. Record both versions’ results.
test: Exchange the final drawing and prototype. Ask a partner to reproduce a critical dimension and explain its purpose.
exit: Show one measured improvement or unresolved limit. Include the earlier result and the new one.
guide: Check the individual measurement and the team handoff separately. A documented limit is valid.

title: Define the problem for a mixed-use building
kit: Per pair, one measuring tape, pencil and ruler. Give each student the four-page Task 2.1 packet. Choose a safe straight walking path and a teacher-approved room.
entry: Start here with the current MVP class. No organizer or previous project is needed. Read Peter Park, Redesigning America, printed pp. 83–87.
measure: Walk ten normal steps. Measure that distance in feet. Repeat three times. Average the distances and divide by ten to find feet per step. A partner can measure or use a tape directly for the room survey.
plan: Pace the room length and width, convert both to feet, and multiply to estimate floor area. Check one dimension with a tape. Mark any difference and the unit.
make: Choose a local site. Sketch a ground floor with housing access and one business or community service. Label entrances and uses. Trace one real trip from a dwelling entrance to that service.
test: Exchange sketches. Have a partner trace the trip without help and point out a barrier. Revise an entrance or route. Record a criterion, a constraint and the reason for the change on your packet.
exit: What local need does your building meet? Give a room dimension or area with units. Use one idea from Peter Park and one detail from your sketch to justify a design decision.
guide: Warm-up example: ten steps covering 24 ft give 2.4 ft/step. An 8-step by 10-step space is about 19.2 ft × 24 ft, or 460.8 ft². Use students’ own measurements for the actual brief. Look for housing plus a service and a route a person can use.

title: Trace the loads a building must carry
kit: Mixed-use building sketch or the packet example, stacked books as supports, card strip and identical washers.
entry: Bring the mixed-use sketch or use a two-floor example with a shop below apartments.
measure: Count a model deck’s self-weight as a permanent load. Mark where you will add equal test masses.
plan: Draw arrows from one person or object through floor, beam, support, and foundation.
make: Span two low supports with the strip. Add a light load first at the center, then near one support. Keep the span fixed.
test: Record the change in bend at both positions. Separate the added live load from the model’s own weight.
exit: Trace one load on your building sketch to the ground. Which part carries it next, and why?
guide: Keep the load small and the setup low. A load path must continue through connections to a support.

title: Build a tower and examine its first failure
kit: Equal sets of paper or card strips, tape, ruler, low test tray, identical light loads.
entry: Agree on a common tower height, stock allowance and test conditions. Write them on the packet before building.
measure: Measure the base and tower height. Record the starting lean or displacement.
plan: Sketch the bracing. Predict which joint or member will move first and how you will see it.
make: Build a freestanding tower to the recorded height using the class material limit. Have a partner check dimensions before loading.
test: Load in equal increments under teacher supervision. Stop at the first major lean or joint slip. Photograph or sketch that first failure.
exit: Identify the first failure and the load or trial when it appeared. What one change follows from it?
guide: Observe from beside the tower. Distinguish the cause from damage that occurred after collapse.

title: Compare construction materials under load
kit: Equal-length samples, two low supports, lightweight identical loads, ruler.
entry: Use the same span and loading point for every sample. Pilot a safe limit before class.
measure: Measure each sample’s span, width, and thickness. Record differences that affect the comparison.
plan: Draw the setup with the loading point and a reference line for deflection.
make: Load the samples one increment at a time. Measure center deflection at a common load. Unload and inspect.
test: Compare which sample bent and recovered, which kept a bend, and which failed. Identify the limits of the comparison.
exit: Recommend a member for one part of your model. Cite a common-load measurement and describe the material response.
guide: A stiffer specimen bends less at equal load. A single geometry test does not prove intrinsic material strength.

title: Test insulation for the building envelope
kit: Matched containers or test boxes, insulation samples, thermometers, timer, teacher-prepared warm water and tray.
entry: Compare a plain enclosure with one insulated enclosure. Use identical containers of teacher-supplied warm water. Match starting amounts and temperatures, then measure at the same intervals.
measure: Record starting temperature, volume, and elapsed time. Identify the one insulation feature to change.
plan: Draw the boundary of the box. Predict a heat-loss path and mark the thermometer location.
make: Prepare a baseline and insulated case. Record temperatures at equal intervals, using the same method.
test: Compare temperature drops after the same interval. Seal one suspected gap and repeat if the starting conditions can be matched.
exit: Which enclosure lost less thermal energy under your test conditions? Support your inference with two measured temperature changes.
guide: Compare like masses and materials. Record a difference in starting conditions rather than silently treating it as equal.

title: Draw the building at a usable scale
kit: Site brief, measured dimensions, grid paper, ruler and pencil.
entry: Provide a measured sketch from 2.1 or a dimensioned site brief.
measure: Choose and label a scale. At 1/2 in = 1 ft, a 12-ft wall occupies 6 in. Convert one real dimension independently.
plan: Mark a common corner. Draw exterior walls, doors, and the two uses. Include a legend and units.
make: Add an elevation or detail showing a feature the floor plan cannot show. Mark the pedestrian route.
test: Give the drawing to another crew. Ask them to recover a real dimension and trace the entrance without asking you.
exit: Show one scale conversion in both directions. What did the partner’s check make you change?
guide: Look for consistent scale and a dimension another reader can recover. Add a scale bar if useful.

title: Construct the mixed-use building model
kit: Scale plan, cardboard, stable base, tape, ruler, scissors and test records.
entry: Use a checked scale plan. Bring your structural and insulation findings to the bench.
measure: Measure wall and opening sizes from the drawing. Mark the model dimensions on a cut list.
plan: Plan a removable roof or open side so reviewers can trace circulation. Identify one evidence-based construction detail.
make: Make the shell, entrances, and interior divisions. Label housing access and the business/service. Add the structural or thermal detail you chose.
test: Let another team follow the route and compare two model dimensions with the plan. Flag one mismatch for revision.
exit: Which feature of the model represents a test result? Give the result and show where it changed the construction.
guide: Inspect the model against the team’s client brief. Appearance alone does not show function.

title: Review the building with its users
kit: Model, plan, scale rule, user brief, test records and repair stock.
entry: Have the building model available. Offer a completed sample for a student entering at review.
measure: Measure the feature flagged at handover and compare with the planned value.
plan: Ask one reviewer to act as a resident and another as a service user. Write a testable concern from each.
make: Revise a feature that addresses one concern. Mark the as-built change on the plan.
test: Repeat the route or fit check. Present the final area, one physical test, and one trade-off.
exit: Defend one change to the client using a measurement, a drawing detail, and an idea from the reading.
guide: Ask for individual scale or load-path checks alongside the team’s presentation. Optional 2.6 concrete testing belongs in a flex block with sufficient curing time.

title: Decode the original boat patent
kit: Piot patent drawing linked in the lesson, pencil, working teacher-tested boat or demonstration, basin and timer.
entry: Enter with Piot’s drawing and a demonstration of the baseline boat. Read the patent as historical engineering evidence.
measure: Trace the engine tubes and mark the waterline on a copy you draw. Pick a fixed travel distance for later tests.
plan: Identify the existing design, the function to preserve, and one measurable improvement. Label each separately.
make: Observe a teacher-run demonstration. Sketch the motion and identify which explanations are observations and which are inferences.
test: Swap annotated sketches. Have a partner trace water into and out of the mechanism and identify one part needing inspection.
exit: What would count as an improvement on this patent? Give a metric and the starting conditions you will keep.
guide: Teacher rehearses basin, flame control, leak checks and storage before release of construction. If heat equipment is unavailable, use the original fluid and press tasks as the practical route.

title: Fabricate and inspect the baseline boat
kit: Teacher-prepared pattern or pilot sample for this equipment, prepared sharp parts, hull stock, tubing, adhesive, eye protection and marked storage.
entry: Use the original boat only with a locally approved and teacher-piloted setup. Without it, start 3.3–3.4.
measure: Take cut, fold and opening dimensions from the teacher-approved station pattern or pilot sample. Record the units and check the paired measurements before forming.
plan: Record the demonstrated station sequence. Mark which steps require an adult, inspection or curing time.
make: At supervised stations, follow the teacher-piloted sequence for the baseline hull and engine. Label and store parts for the adhesive cure time posted at the station.
test: Inspect alignment, sealed seams, tube clearance, and hull symmetry. Have the teacher sign off before a powered basin test.
exit: Explain one quality check that must happen before the next assembly step. Locate it on your drawing.
guide: Use prepared metal edges and approved equipment. Allow the adhesive’s full cure and require the local preheat inspection.

title: Establish the boat baseline and compare fluids
kit: Inspected boat, marked basin, timer, teacher-controlled heat station, needle-free syringes, matching tubing and tray.
entry: Use a fully cured and inspected boat. A second group can investigate syringes while awaiting its basin turn.
measure: Mark start and finish lines. Record distance, time, load and test conditions for three comparable runs.
plan: Predict what changes when linked syringes contain air instead of water. Mark the initial piston positions.
make: Run the approved baseline boat at the teacher station. At the fluid station move the input piston a fixed distance and measure the output travel.
test: Repeat each fluid trial. Look for bubbles, slipping tubing, or a changed load before interpreting differences.
exit: Give one baseline boat speed or a syringe travel comparison. Explain what you held constant and why.
guide: Record failed starts separately. If using the press route, collect actual fluid trials and keep boat observations distinct.

title: Build and test a manufacturing press
kit: Two sizes of needle-free syringes, snug tubing, tray, stand, soft test sample, ruler.
entry: Start with working leak-checked pairs. Show how to release pressure and keep fingers out of the press.
measure: Measure input and output piston travel with the same reference edge. Record syringe sizes.
plan: Draw the input piston, tube, output piston, and load. Predict the effect of swapping the syringe sizes.
make: Mount the connected syringes so an input stroke drives the output piston against a soft sample. Keep hands clear. Swap roles to inspect the mechanism.
test: Run three equal input strokes in both arrangements. Compare output travel and the change in the sample.
exit: Which arrangement met the job better? Include travel measurements and identify the trade-off.
guide: Do not infer a force value from travel alone. On the equipment-limited route, retain this press for a measured redesign.

title: Explain the heat engine cycle
kit: Packet cycle grid, tested teacher boat or approved heat-engine demonstration, colored pencils.
entry: Use the teacher demonstration and the cycle prompts in the packet. Distinguish what you saw from what you inferred.
measure: Mark heat input, surrounding cooler water, and tube openings. Identify where the team observed water motion.
plan: Draw successive states of the working fluid. Predict the direction of flow at two points in the cycle.
make: Watch the approved demonstration. Annotate the cycle with changes in temperature, pressure, and movement. Discuss which changes are inferred.
test: Have a partner trace the entire cycle back to its starting state. Repair a missing energy transfer or reversed arrow.
exit: Use two stages in the cycle to explain how heating can produce repeated motion. Identify evidence and one inference.
guide: Use teacher-controlled heat sources only. The press route demonstrates fluid transmission, not heat-engine performance.

title: Test fluid flow and thrust
kit: Different lengths of equal-bore tubing, reservoir or syringe with controlled drive, container, timer, tray.
entry: At a contained fluid station, compare two tube routes under the same drive. Choose just one difference and record it on the packet.
measure: Mark a common head or driving condition. Measure tube length, collection time, and collected volume.
plan: Draw two routes differing in one variable. Predict which will deliver more water in equal time.
make: Run both routes from the same starting condition. Keep tube ends and water level consistent. Collect three trials.
test: Calculate volume/time with units. Check for kinks or changing head. Compare the direction of an outlet jet with the expected reaction.
exit: Which change would you recommend testing on the boat or press? Support your prediction with measured flow rates.
guide: Do not use flow alone to claim a faster boat. Recheck the changed machine under the original performance test.

title: Design and build the boat revision
kit: Working baseline boat or press, test record, replacement stock, ruler and annotated drawing.
entry: Start only with a functioning baseline and an actual test record. If entering here, run the baseline first.
measure: Choose one dimension or operating condition you can change. Measure the initial value and set a target.
plan: Sketch the revision and predict how it will change the selected metric. Keep the other test conditions fixed.
make: Build one change under the same equipment approvals. Inspect and allow cure time before retesting. On the press route change one linkage or syringe arrangement.
test: Run an unpowered inspection or leak test first. Have a second person check that the original test can still be repeated.
exit: What did you change, what stayed fixed, and what numerical outcome would support your prediction?
guide: Separate an intended design change from a repair required only to make the original work.

title: Retest under the baseline conditions
kit: Inspected revised boat or press, original setup and test log, timer or ruler.
entry: Bring both versions’ dimensions and the original trial method. Allow extra time if curing is incomplete.
measure: Use the same course length or input stroke, same load, and same start rule. Collect at least three revised trials.
plan: Make a two-column table for baseline and revision. Write the units at the top.
make: Run the revised machine, recording every attempt. Calculate the same measure used for the baseline.
test: Compare typical values and spread. If a trial fails, describe the cause you observed before excluding it.
exit: Does the data support your improvement claim? Include both values, units, and a limit of the comparison.
guide: For a speed claim compare distance/time. For a time claim over fixed distance, shorter can be better. Ask students to state the criterion.

title: Present an improvement claim
kit: Revised device, labeled drawing, data table and the presentation checks on this packet.
entry: Prepare a classroom patent presentation with diagrams, test evidence, and a change from an existing design.
measure: Check every labeled dimension and compare the claim with the recorded before-and-after results.
plan: Organize the presentation around the original need, change, mechanism, and evidence. Assign a speaking role to each team member.
make: Demonstrate the working device using the approved setup. Give a peer the drawing and ask them to locate the modified feature.
test: Respond to one challenge about the mechanism or test. Revise an overstrong claim using the actual measurements.
exit: Which evidence supports your claim, and which question would need another test?
guide: Collect the individual mechanism explanation. A press improvement is reported as a press result. Treat this as a classroom presentation.

title: Send a scoreboard digit with a shared code
kit: Matched low-voltage cell, lamp, switch, leads, scoreboard diagram and paper segment cards.
entry: Enter with an inspected low-voltage kit. First show a complete switched loop. Never use wall power.
measure: Mark the segment positions A–G in the same order on two cards. Count which segments light for one digit.
plan: Make an on/off code for digits 0–9. Agree on the bit order and the meaning of 1 and 0.
make: Build a switched lamp circuit. One partner sends three secret digit patterns and the other reconstructs the display.
test: Swap roles and decode three new patterns. If a digit is wrong, compare segment order before changing the key.
exit: Show the code for one digit and explain how another person can decode it without seeing your drawing.
guide: Observe both sender and receiver. An invertible, consistent code is more important than its particular notation.

title: Design a mouse detector and test false alarms
kit: Matched low-voltage kit, switch or sensor, lamp or buzzer, insulated leads, paper trigger and student packet.
entry: Use a paper model to simulate movement. Test the output component with the battery before adding a trigger.
measure: Set the trigger location and record how many trials you will run with and without movement.
plan: Draw the source, trigger, and output. State what should happen in each condition.
make: Assemble the detector and move the simulated trigger the same way for each trial. Record the output.
test: Run three trigger and three no-trigger trials. Change one unreliable contact. Repeat both sets.
exit: Give the detector’s true detections and false alarms. Which change would improve reliability?
guide: Separate missed detections from false alarms. Reuse the door-signal board as a troubleshooting station.

title: Build a sender and receiver
kit: Teacher-tested low-voltage communication kit, transmitter and receiver or paired lamp and switch, screen and message cards.
entry: Check a complete working sender and receiver before class. Rotate teams if only one kit is available.
measure: Measure or mark a fixed separation. Agree on a small message set and the start/stop signal.
plan: Draw the sender, channel, and receiver. Mark the point where the message changes form.
make: Send messages chosen out of sight of the receiver. Use the audio or optical stages of the available communication kit. A coded lamp is a classroom substitute.
test: Record decoded messages out of total attempts. Compare one changed condition at the same distance.
exit: Where did information change form? Use a decoded message or error to support your explanation.
guide: A glowing transmitter is not proof of successful reception. Require a blind receiver trial.

title: Plan communications for a lunar base
kit: Lunar-base brief in the packet, prior communication test and pencil.
entry: Use a working link from the previous task or supply its measured performance and state its limits.
measure: Mark sender, receiver, and the medium for each required route. Compare indoor, surface, and long-distance links.
plan: Choose a channel for each route. Give one reason related to environment, range, or obstruction.
make: Create the system diagram and label conversions. Demonstrate an Earth-classroom model of one message path where equipment permits.
test: Ask another team to follow a message from origin to destination. Identify an obstruction, failed component, or missing return path.
exit: Defend one channel choice and explain a limit of your classroom test for the lunar setting.
guide: Sound needs a material medium. Require a plausible link across vacuum and distinguish a design from a working demonstration.

title: Measure current in a lamp branch
kit: Supervised matched battery and lamp kit, correctly configured ammeter, leads and schematic.
entry: Teacher checks range, meter port, and meter fuse. Power off before changing a connection.
measure: Trace the closed lamp path. Identify where you will break the branch and what unit you expect.
plan: Draw the meter in series. Have a partner and teacher check the drawing and connection before energizing.
make: Take a current reading. Switch power off, move the meter to a second point in the same unbranched loop, then measure again.
test: Compare readings and their precision. Investigate a large difference by checking range, battery and contacts.
exit: Where did you insert the meter and why? Report two readings and what the comparison shows.
guide: Never connect an ammeter across the battery. Use teacher-supplied data only as analysis if the live meter station is unavailable.

title: Map voltage differences
kit: Matched battery, two lamps, voltmeter or multimeter set for DC voltage, leads and diagram.
entry: Review meter roles. Use a teacher-approved low-voltage source and a stable circuit.
measure: Record the source voltage across its terminals. Label measurement points on a schematic.
plan: Predict the voltage across a lamp and across a closed connection. Mark both meter leads for each prediction.
make: Connect the voltmeter in parallel at each pair of points. Record the setting, sign, and units.
test: Reverse the leads on one measurement. Explain the sign change and compare the voltage drops round a closed loop.
exit: Show one lead placement and explain what the number measures between those two points.
guide: A voltage reading belongs to a pair of points. Verify that the leads and dial are in voltage mode.

title: Design the fan control circuit
kit: Matched low-voltage motor and guarded fan, switch/controller and kit-specified components, schematic.
entry: Use a tested motor kit, a clear guard, and teacher-approved current limits. Disconnect power for rewiring.
measure: List the required speeds and directions in a state table. Mark the intended polarity at the motor for each direction.
plan: Draw a circuit for each switch state. Trace the current path and identify the component changing the speed.
make: Use the teacher-checked diagram for the available kit. Build one state at a time. Verify direction and two distinct speed settings before combining the controls.
test: Ask a partner to predict the motor state from the diagram before operating it. Record differences and disconnect power before correcting a connection.
exit: Which control changes direction and which changes speed in your circuit? Support it with an observation.
guide: If the motor station is missing, schedule a rotation and record the physical fan check as pending. A two-room light model can rehearse switches.

title: Commission the fan controller
kit: Fan controller, packet operating table, approved spare parts and labels.
entry: Bring the checked controller. If entering here, provide an assembled control system and its circuit drawing.
measure: Mark a safe stop position and identify how to tell forward from reverse. Use the same method to compare speeds.
plan: Write a test for every required control state. Include a safe power-off check.
make: One partner operates the controls from the labels while another reads the schematic. Exchange roles. Repair one fault or labeling problem.
test: Retest both speeds and reversal. Give the control sheet to a neighboring crew and ask them to reproduce a selected state.
exit: Name the failed or unclear state, the correction, and the observed outcome after retesting.
guide: Observe the actual device. If a state was not demonstrated, leave that criterion pending.

title: Choose a power source for a lighthouse
kit: Island lighthouse design brief and source comparison in the student packet, plus a calculator.
entry: Design for the 1,000 W lighthouse lamp on an isolated island. State the night length, compare power options, and account for storage and maintenance.
measure: Compute daily demand as lamp power × operating hours. Example: 10 W for 12 h uses 120 Wh. Keep W and Wh distinct.
plan: Compare two candidate supplies. Include operating hours, storage, site conditions, and an assumption.
make: Prepare a proposal with a labeled energy-flow diagram, demand estimate, and a plan for hours when the source is unavailable.
test: Have a partner change one condition such as a longer night. Recalculate and revise the recommendation.
exit: What source and storage plan would you recommend? Cite one calculated demand and one site constraint.
guide: A nameplate power rating alone cannot guarantee daily delivery. Optional Task 4.8 extends this work to a consumer device.

pages: Return to the selected project task
title: Repair and retest a project
kit: Selected team artifact, original data, same test setup, student packet and replacement stock.
entry: Move this meeting to the project that needs another trial. Choose a physical test or, with setup time, the optional concrete or consumer-device investigation.
measure: Measure the current condition. Record the baseline, its units, and the test method before touching the artifact.
plan: Identify one change and predict the direction of its effect. For a concrete extension (2.6), plan batches and full cure before comparing samples.
make: Make the chosen repair or conduct a teacher-approved concrete or low-voltage consumer-device investigation. Record the changed variable and the result in this packet.
test: Repeat the same test. Record a result that confirms or contradicts the prediction and discuss what to try next.
exit: Which piece of evidence changed your decision? Cite the task, measurements, and what you will do next.
guide: Schedule at the point of need. Offer fresh individual checks on measuring, drawing, or the relevant calculation.

pages: Return to the selected project rubric
title: Demonstrate and defend a design
kit: Finished product or model, dated packet test data, drawing, ruler and one-page exhibit label.
entry: Select any ETF project you completed. Bring a test record and the packet or saved lesson evidence that documents the test.
measure: Recheck one dimension or operating value in front of a peer. Write the unit and the acceptance criterion.
plan: Plan a short demonstration that shows the need, mechanism, measured result, and revision.
make: Demonstrate the device or model. Invite a peer to use the drawing to find a feature or operate one state. Rotate roles.
test: Ask the reviewer to challenge one assumption. Demonstrate a repeat trial or explain what additional evidence is needed.
exit: Independently defend a change using a reading idea, a drawing feature, and comparable results from your own tests.
guide: Use the exhibit checks on the student packet. Rate each student’s actual math, measurement, plan reading and design explanation separately.
